7be20f7bc3.facts:
Headline: Drift Protocol Exploit Wallets Move $61.6 Million in Ether to Tornado Cash
Sources: Decrypt, Yahoo Finance, www.tokenpost.com

Article text:
Wallets tied to April's $295 million Drift Protocol exploit pushed 25,700 Ethereum, worth about $61.56 million, into the crypto mixer Tornado Cash over roughly two hours on Tuesday. The addresses had been quiet for about two months before the burst. Transfer data from Arkham Intelligence shows the deposits landing in batches of 100 ETH, about $237,800 each, plus smaller 10 ETH chunks. Those sizes match the mixer's fixed deposit pools, which let users pull funds out later from fresh addresses and break the public link between sender and receiver. Arkham's entity page, which tracks 71 addresses linked to the attacker, still shows 81,454 ETH sitting in those wallets after Tuesday's deposits, worth roughly $198.58 million at current prices. Besides that ETH stash, the wallet holds around $561.6K in other coins like USDT, USDC, Solana, and USDY. Tuesday's deposits follow a first round on July 23 and 24, when an address labeled Drift Exploiter 4 sent about 23,095 ETH, then worth around $44.4 million, into the same mixer. The April 1 exploit hit Drift's vaults on Solana after the attacker gained admin powers, introduced a fake token and used it to borrow out real liquidity. Drift's own asset breakdown puts the haul at $295.7 million, led by $159.3 million in JLP—the Jupiter Liquidity Provider token—and $71.4 million in USDC, most of which was later swapped and bridged to Ethereum. Arkham's portfolio view still lists exactly one Fartcoin in the exploiter's holdings, worth about 15 cents, a long way from the $4.1 million in Fartcoin that Drift says was taken in April. Drift said in April that the attack was a six-month operation in which the group posed as a quantitative trading firm, met contributors in person and deposited $1 million of its own money to build trust. In June, Drift said forensic firm Mandiant attributed the attack to UNC6862, a North Korean threat group. The recovery pool held about 3.1 million USDT at launch, so early redemptions paid roughly 0.0104 USDT per token, or about a penny on the dollar. The pool gets a daily cut of between 60% and 90% of Velocity's net protocol revenue, scaling up as daily revenue grows, and Tether has committed up to 127.5 million USDT toward the relaunch and recovery. New York AG seeks $1.37 billion from NovaTech founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion: $1.13 billion in disgorgement plus $232.5 million in prejudgment interest. New York Attorney General Letitia James has asked a court to order defunct crypto and forex trading platform NovaTech’s founders, Cynthia and Eddy Petion, and related companies to pay $1.37 billion over its Ponzi scheme. The AG is seeking the return of about $1.13 billion in investor funds, plus $232.5 million in interest, according to a Thursday court filing. The court found the Petions and the companies liable by default in August 2025 after they failed to respond to the lawsuit. Four people who recruited investors into NovaTech have separately agreed to pay nearly $6 million in settlements intended to benefit victims, according to the AG’s office. More than 11,000 New Yorkers lost tens of millions of dollars through NovaTech and an earlier crypto mining scheme, AWS Mining, the AG’s office said. The complaint alleged that promoters targeted Haitian and other immigrant communities through prayer groups, social media and WhatsApp, promising high returns and recruitment bonuses. The filing says that investors deposited about $1.16 billion into NovaTech’s crypto wallets between August 2019 and May 2023. Of that, only about $26 million was deposited with the platform’s trading provider, B2Broker, for trading, according to the attorney general. The motion separately seeks about $6.15 million, including interest, over AWS Mining. AWS Mining collapsed in 2019. NovaTech collapsed in 2023, leaving tens of thousands of investors unable to withdraw their funds. James sued NovaTech, AWS Mining and other associated companies in June 2024. Cointelegraph sought comment from the New York Attorney General’s Office on how any recovered funds would be distributed to victims and what steps could be taken to enforce the judgment, but had not received a response by publication. Headline: Swiss regulator FINMA approves country’s first spot bitcoin ETF for retail investors
Sources: The Block, The Defiant, TradingView

Article text:
Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here. Swiss regulator FINMA approves country's first spot bitcoin ETF for retail investorsSwitzerland already has bitcoin exchange-traded products, but the newly approved ETF falls under a different regulatory framework for investment funds. ShareQuick Take

Switzerland’s financial regulator FINMA has approved its first retail ETF that invests directly in bitcoin, with other fund providers also seeking approval.
FINMA made an exception to its diversification rules for the bitcoin ETF and outlined safeguards for custody, operational risks, and investor disclosures.

Switzerland's financial regulator FINMA has approved the country's first spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund for retail investors, allowing a fund to invest directly in the cryptocurrency under Swiss investment fund rules. The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority said Tuesday that the ETF falls into the category of "other funds for alternative investments" with a specific risk under Swiss law. Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) has a longer trading history and much higher trading volumes than most other cryptocurrencies, FINMA said, which allowed it to make an exception to the rules requiring funds to diversify their investments. Other fund providers have also submitted or announced applications for bitcoin ETFs, the regulator said. Switzerland is no stranger to exchange-traded crypto investments. The SIX Swiss Exchange has listed bitcoin exchange-traded products (ETPs) for years, including a bitcoin and ether product launched in 2019. FINMA also authorized a crypto fund for qualified investors in 2021. Existing Swiss bitcoin ETPs are debt securities, rather than investment funds. FINMA's newly approved ETF falls under Swiss fund law, with rules covering custody, operational risks, and investor disclosures. A FINMA spokesperson declined to identify the approved fund or its issuer when contacted by The Block, saying it does not provide institution-specific information. FINMA's January guidance set out the operational and custody risks associated with crypto investments. FINMA said supervised institutions must take measures to mitigate those risks and clearly explain them in fund documents, with the Financial Services Act rules of conduct applying when the ETF is sold. FINMA said approving the ETF does not change the risks of investing in bitcoin. The cryptocurrency remains highly volatile, and investors could lose a significant portion of their money, it said.

Headline: OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban
Sources: CoinDesk, Cointelegraph, The Block, Wu Blockchain

Telegram news posts about it:
OCC Finalizes First GENIUS Act Rule: No Safe Harbor for Existing Stablecoin Rewards

The OCC has issued its first final rule implementing the GENIUS Act, covering stablecoin issuance, custody, and third-party partnerships, effective January 18, 2027. Existing yield and rewards programs receive no automatic grandfathering or safe harbor; compliance will be assessed case by case.

The act prohibits issuers from paying yield solely for holding, using, or retaining stablecoins, but does not ban all third-party rewards. The OCC said rewards based at least partly on other factors may fall outside the prohibition. The implications for programs offered by Coinbase, PayPal, and Kraken remain uncertain. — link
🇺🇸 BREAKING: The US OCC finalizes GENIUS Act rules for stablecoin issuers, covering reserves, redemptions, and custody.

Effective January 18, 2027.

News | Markets | YouTube
Article text:
5 min readMake  preferred on ShareShare this articleCopy linkX iconX (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmailMake  preferred on Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould (Nikhilesh De/CoinDesk) SummaryShowThe U.S. agency that regulates national banks and trusts has issued the first final rule putting the GENIUS Act into place in January, though a number of other regulators are still working on other parts of the implementation.The section on stablecoin yield doesn't offer a lot of detail on what activity may fall under the law's wide prohibition of such yield from issuers, but the crypto industry has already interpreted GENIUS to permit the rewards programs that have become commonplace with stablecoin activity on exchanges.The final rule states that pre-existing rewards programs won't get special treatment as the OCC assesses which ones pass regulatory muster.U.S. crypto exchanges that have long been giving people rewards for usings stablecoins will have to get the agency to sign off on those existing programs, according to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the first federal banking regulator to issue a final rule under the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act. The OCC, which oversees U.S. national banks and trusts that will play a central role in the issuance of stablecoins under the law, issued a final rule on Wednesday to establish the regulations under which the firms that issue the dollar-based tokens will operate — including in their third-party relationships with the exchanges on which their stablecoins change hands. The agency — an independent bureau of the Treasury Department — has declined to offer examples or illustrations of what type of rewards operations may run afoul of the GENIUS Act, which declared that payments to customers made "solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin" won't be allowed. The industry, which won't get any safe harbors for existing programs, will just have to test the agency's case-by-case oversight to get a better sense of the rule, which is set to go live on January 18. The regulator said it "will apply the language of the statute to the facts and circumstances of any particular arrangement." However, the agency did suggest that the word "solely" in the prohibition is carrying a lot of weight, and that a reward that "might be made, at least in part, for other reasons" would fall outside the ban in the GENIUS Act. Payment stablecoins hew to the value of the U.S. dollar and are designed — as suggested by the name — to maintain a steady value in a crypto industry in which other assets are known to be famously volatile. The sector is currently led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, but a number of entrants have begun crowding into the space.
